name: mimalloc
workload: mimalloc-bench suite (cfrac, leanN Lean theorem-prover self-build, redis, larsonN, mstressN, rptestN, alloc-test, sh6bench/sh8bench, xmalloc-testN, cache-scratch) run on a 16-core AMD 5950x and a 36-core (2x18) Intel Xeon c5.18xlarge
claimed_speedup: sh6bench: mimalloc "more than 2.5x faster than jemalloc"; sh8bench: tcmalloc becomes "10x slower than before" once thread migration is added (mimalloc does not regress); leanN real-world compile workload: "13% speedup over tcmalloc", conjectured up to 1.6x when normalized for allocator time share; xmalloc-testN: mimalloc "outperforms others by a very large margin"
compiler_and_flags: GCC 9.3.0 (AMD 5950x run) / Clang 10.0.0 (Xeon c5.18xlarge run); the companion mimalloc-bench build scripts (github.com/daanx/mimalloc-bench, build-bench-env.sh) use CFLAGS/CXXFLAGS='-march=native' plus per-allocator -O2/-O3
hardware: 16-core AMD Ryzen 5950x (Zen3) 3.4GHz/4.9GHz boost, 32GiB 3600MHz RAM, Ubuntu 20.04, glibc 2.31; also reported on a 36-core 2x18-core Intel Xeon Cascade Lake (AWS c5.18xlarge), 144GiB RAM
stars_or_usage: 13.4k stars; used in Azure, Bing, Unreal Engine, Death Stranding PC, SPAdes
tradeoffs: secure-mode build (guard pages, encrypted free lists) costs ~10% avg perf penalty; eager purge/decommit trades some memory-release syscall overhead for lower steady-state RSS; not every benchmark favors it (cfrac/redis roughly tie jemalloc/tcmalloc)
caveats: The chart data (SVG bar charts in doc/bench-2021/) also includes glibc 2.31 as a tested allocator and mimalloc leads it in almost every benchmark, but the exact glibc-specific numbers are only rendered as vector-graphic bars, not extractable as page text, so per the hard rule that every claimed_speedup number must appear as text on the page, glibc is not used as the cited baseline here -- jemalloc/tcmalloc are used since those specific ratios are quoted in prose. README itself flags the 2021-01-30 data as dated: "many of these allocators have improved over time as well. YMMV."
found_via: seed-record pass: github.com/microsoft/mimalloc README (#Performance section) plus the linked github.com/daanx/mimalloc-bench suite

name: jemalloc
baseline: phkmalloc (FreeBSD libc malloc, the incumbent jemalloc replaced)
workload: malloc-test microbenchmark (Lever & Boreham 2000): tight alloc/dealloc loop, 40,000,000 cycles total divided across up to 20 threads, one 512-byte object per cycle; plus five single-threaded real programs (cca, cfrac, GhostScript, sh6bench, smlng) and a MySQL super-smack query-throughput benchmark
claimed_speedup: Single-threaded programs (mean run time, phkmalloc vs jemalloc, from the paper's tables): cca 77.73s vs 69.37s (~1.12x, derived from page data); gs 42.48s vs 34.24s (~1.24x, derived from page data); sh6bench 6.96s vs 4.50s (~1.55x, derived from page data); smlng 13.89s vs 11.49s (~1.21x, derived from page data). Multi-threaded malloc-test: jemalloc sustains roughly 2x10^7 allocations/sec flat out to 20 threads while phkmalloc collapses to roughly 1-2x10^5 allocations/sec by 10 threads (~100x, derived from page data, approximate reading of the log-scale Figure 6 plot)
hardware: four-processor system (dual-dual AMD Opteron 275), FreeBSD-CURRENT/amd64, April 2006
stars_or_usage: 11.2k stars; default allocator for FreeBSD libc, used by Redis, historically Firefox, and many large-scale services at Meta
tradeoffs: multiple arenas reduce contention but can raise peak memory in low-concurrency cases; larger tuning surface (narenas, dirty/muzzy decay_ms, percpu_arena); jemalloc's own README/TUNING.md carries no numeric benchmarks
caveats: The strongest quantitative evidence found is jemalloc's own founding paper (Evans, 'A Scalable Concurrent malloc(3) Implementation for FreeBSD', BSDCan 2006), which compares against phkmalloc (FreeBSD's contemporary libc malloc), not glibc malloc directly -- baseline recorded honestly as phkmalloc per the rules, baseline_in_list=false. Numbers are ~20 years old, hardware and allocator versions are long obsolete, and the paper states benchmark code/graphing tool are 'available upon request' rather than linked, so this is capped at Tier B rather than A. No modern (post-2010) numeric jemalloc-vs-glibc benchmark with stated methodology was found within the tool budget; jemalloc's own repo (README, TUNING.md) contains no benchmark numbers at all.
found_via: seed-record pass: github.com/jemalloc/jemalloc wiki Background page -> BSDCan 2006 paper PDF (people.freebsd.org/~jasone/jemalloc/bsdcan2006/jemalloc.pdf)

name: snmalloc
workload: ISMM 2019 paper micro-benchmarks: a symmetric workload (each thread allocates, swaps with another thread, and deallocates) and a producer/consumer workload (malloc-test, half the threads allocate batches of 4096 objects sized 8-2048B, the other half deallocate), swept from 1 to 64 threads; also a SPECspeed 2017 Integer suite run and two real-application integrations (FaRM, FreeBSD libc)
claimed_speedup: Figures 4-6 (allocations/sec vs thread count and vs object size, 16B-32KiB): glibc is consistently among the lowest throughput lines, while snmalloc/snmalloc-1mib are near the top; e.g. in the 1KiB-32KiB producer/consumer sweep snmalloc sustains roughly 150-200M allocs/sec at 64 threads vs glibc under 50M allocs/sec, on the order of 3-4x (derived from page data, approximate reading of the Figure 5/6 charts -- no single ratio is stated verbatim in the paper's prose). Separately, FreeBSD 12.0 replaced jemalloc with snmalloc as libc's default malloc with only 24 added lines, a qualitative deployment datapoint, not a vs-glibc number.
hardware: Symmetric/producer-consumer micro-benchmarks: Ubuntu 18.04 Azure Standard_F64s_v2 VM (64 vCPUs, 128GB RAM); object-size sweep: dual-socket Intel Xeon Platinum 8168; SPECspeed suite: Azure Standard_D3_v2 (4 vCPUs, 14GB RAM, Intel Xeon E5-2673)
stars_or_usage: 2.0k stars; default allocator in FreeBSD libc since 12.0, used via the snmalloc-rs crate in Rust
tradeoffs: message-passing remote deallocation adds an outgoing-buffer/batching mechanism (tunable, default 1MiB) which trades a little memory for throughput; higher implementation complexity than simple thread-caching allocators; paper notes SuperMalloc needed >100s to reach peak throughput while snmalloc/glibc/rpmalloc warm up in about 20s
caveats: Exact numeric speedup ratios for snmalloc vs glibc are read off log-scale throughput charts (Figures 4-6), not stated as an explicit ratio in the paper's prose, so the figure above is derived/approximate rather than a verbatim quote -- flagged accordingly. Paper is peer-reviewed (ACM ISMM '19) and code is public at the cited repo, but the exact compiler and optimization flags used for the micro-benchmarks were not found in the extracted pages, so this is capped at Tier B rather than A. snmalloc's own README states the implementation "has evolved significantly since the initial paper... most of the meta-data layout has changed", so current performance may differ from the 2019 figures.
found_via: seed-record pass: github.com/microsoft/snmalloc README -> snmalloc.pdf (Lietar et al., 'snmalloc: A Message Passing Allocator', ISMM 2019)

name: gperftools TCMalloc
workload: single malloc/free round-trip for small objects, single-threaded, as described in TCMalloc's original design writeup
claimed_speedup: "ptmalloc2 takes approximately 300 nanoseconds to execute a malloc/free pair on a 2.8 GHz P4 (for small objects). The TCMalloc implementation takes approximately 50 nanoseconds for the same operation pair." (~6x faster, verbatim from docs/tcmalloc.adoc Motivation section)
stars_or_usage: 9.0k stars; historically used in Chrome/Chromium, widely packaged as libtcmalloc in Linux distros
tradeoffs: ~1% space overhead for small objects claimed vs ptmalloc2's larger per-object header/rounding overhead (same doc); per-thread caches can strand memory across allocation phases if arenas mismatch; project's own current maintainer notes glibc has since closed much of this original gap
caveats: Numbers are from the original ~2005 TCMalloc design writeup, kept verbatim in current docs with an explicit 2024 editor's warning: "referenced glibc versions are now long obsolete. And amount of time per malloc call is far from correct anymore. And the description is for 32-bit computers." No compiler, flags, or reproducible benchmark harness are given (project's own partial-methodology claim), so this is capped at Tier C rather than B, per the rule that the project's own benchmark code/claims with partial methodology is C, not B.

name: TCMalloc (google/tcmalloc)
workload: No specific benchmark named; docs/overview.md frames TCMalloc as "an alternative to the one provided by the C standard library (on Linux usually through glibc)" and states it is "designed to be more efficient at scale than other implementations", without a stated test.
stars_or_usage: 5.4k stars; used throughout Google's production C++ services
tradeoffs: hard dependency on Abseil; default per-CPU caching fast path requires Linux RSEQ support (kernel >=4.18), else falls back to slower per-thread caching; heavier build/dependency footprint than gperftools' tcmalloc
caveats: No public numeric benchmark of google/tcmalloc vs glibc malloc, std::allocator, or operator new/delete was found in the repo's docs within the tool budget, so this is recorded at Tier D on the qualitative overview.md claim. The project DOES have strong peer-reviewed numeric evidence -- Hunter, Kennelly et al., 'Beyond malloc efficiency to fleet efficiency: a hugepage-aware memory allocator' (OSDI 2021, usenix.org/system/files/osdi21-hunter.pdf) -- showing TCMalloc's Temeraire hugepage-aware pageheap beating TCMalloc's OWN prior non-hugepage-aware pageheap by +3.2% average CPU throughput and a reduction in pageheap memory overhead from 14.3% to 10.6% fleet-wide (Table 1, Fig. 15), plus a Redis 6.0.9 case study (+0.75% throughput, +0.44%, on Intel Skylake Xeon, LLVM -O3, 'redis-benchmark' tool, 2000 trials of 1M requests). That comparison is TCMalloc-vs-TCMalloc, not vs any of this project's listed baselines, so per the WHAT COUNTS rules it is not used to set the evidence tier here, but is flagged for the orchestrator in case a TCMalloc-self-improvement category is useful. google/tcmalloc is the documented successor to gperftools' tcmalloc (called 'abseil tcmalloc' in gperftools/docs/tcmalloc.adoc); the direct, quoted glibc comparison lives with the original design and is recorded separately under the 'gperftools TCMalloc' entry.
found_via: seed-record pass: github.com/google/tcmalloc README/docs/overview.md, docs/temeraire.md -> OSDI 2021 paper (usenix.org/system/files/osdi21-hunter.pdf)

name: Eigen
workload: None found against the named baselines -- checked README.md and the doc/ directory (including UsingBlasLapackBackends.dox and DenseDecompositionBenchmark.dox)
claimed_speedup: No throughput/GFLOPS claim against OpenBLAS, Intel MKL, naive loops, or std::valarray was found. Eigen's docs instead position it as a layer that can optionally call OpenBLAS/MKL/Apple Accelerate/Netlib LAPACK as an internal backend (EIGEN_USE_BLAS / EIGEN_USE_LAPACKE macros) rather than claiming to outperform them.
stars_or_usage: 1.2k GitLab stars (project moved off GitHub to GitLab in 2019); foundational dependency of ROS, TensorFlow, Ceres Solver, PCL, OpenCV, g2o, Blender, and many other numerical/robotics/vision projects
tradeoffs: Header-only template library, so heavy expression-template usage can increase compile times; built-in kernels favor small/fixed-size matrices (avoiding BLAS call overhead) while very large dense problems are the case where linking an external BLAS/LAPACK backend is recommended instead of relying solely on Eigen's own kernels.
caveats: Thorough search found no numeric comparison against the seed's named baselines. doc/DenseDecompositionBenchmark.dox does contain a real timing table (Intel Core i7 @ 2.6GHz, clang, AVX+FMA, single precision) but it only compares Eigen's own decomposition algorithms (LLT, LDLT, PartialPivLU, HouseholderQR, JacobiSVD, BDCSVD, ...) against each other, not against OpenBLAS/MKL/naive loops/std::valarray, so it does not satisfy the 'beats a named baseline' requirement. The historically well-known eigen.tuxfamily.org/index.php?title=Benchmark wiki page (cited in numerous papers for GFLOPS vs ATLAS/GOTO/MKL) now permanently redirects to a GitLab Pages mirror that is gated behind a Cloudflare bot challenge and could not be retrieved this session; it likely contains genuine Tier A/B-quality evidence that this pass simply could not access. Recorded at tier D per the 'no numeric comparison found' rule for a project that is unambiguously notable.
found_via: seed-record pass: gitlab.com/libeigen/eigen README and doc/ directory (eigen.tuxfamily.org benchmark wiki attempted but inaccessible)

name: moodycamel::ConcurrentQueue
workload: Producer/consumer microbenchmarks on AWS 8-core (c1.xlarge, Xeon E5506 @2.13GHz) and 32-core (cc2.8xlarge, Xeon E5-2670 @2.60GHz) instances, varying thread counts, comparing moodycamel::ConcurrentQueue (with/without tokens, incl. bulk ops), boost::lockfree::queue, tbb::concurrent_queue, and a std::mutex-locked queue (LockBasedQueue), under balanced mixed producer/consumer and producer-only workloads.
claimed_speedup: Balanced 8-thread workload: moodycamel (with tokens) 795.01k ops/s vs boost::lockfree 647.96k ops/s (~1.2x) vs tbb::concurrent_queue 692.97k ops/s (~1.15x). Producer-only 8-thread throughput: moodycamel 65.56M ops/s vs boost::lockfree 289.71k ops/s (~226x, via bulk enqueue) vs tbb 936.20k ops/s (~70x). Weighted overall average ops/s/thread across all thread counts: moodycamel (incl. bulk) 19.04M vs boost::lockfree 4.07M (~4.7x) vs tbb 5.09M (~3.7x). LockBasedQueue (std::mutex+std::queue) shown separately degrading from 2.6us/op at 2 threads to 112us/op at 16 threads under contention.
compiler_and_flags: g++ on Ubuntu; exact g++ version and optimization flags (-O2/-O3 etc.) not stated on the blog page.
hardware: AWS c1.xlarge: 8-core Intel Xeon E5506 @ 2.13GHz; AWS cc2.8xlarge: 32-core Intel Xeon E5-2670 @ 2.60GHz; Ubuntu
stars_or_usage: 12.5k stars; packaged in vcpkg, used across many C++ game/systems projects
tradeoffs: Not linearizable across independent producers; not NUMA-aware; single-header C++11; the largest speedups (~70-226x) come from its bulk enqueue/dequeue API rather than single-item ops, where the advantage over boost::lockfree is closer to ~1.2x in this benchmark.
caveats: This is a first-party benchmark (author's own blog post plus the repo's own benchmarks/ directory), not an independent suite -- the schema's rule states project's-own-benchmark-with-partial-methodology is tier C, not B. Compiler version and optimization flags are not stated even though CPU models and OS are; the ~226x producer-only figure is a bulk-vs-non-bulk comparison, not like-for-like single-enqueue throughput. Data is from a 2014 blog post and has not been re-verified against current boost/TBB releases this session.

name: liburing
workload: fio random-read IOPS with 1KB blocks across 4 files, 8 CPUs running 72 fio jobs, iodepth=8; tested both direct I/O on NVMe (uncached) and buffered I/O with a hot page cache; a separate single-CPU 512-byte test on Intel Optane measured throughput and latency.
claimed_speedup: Direct I/O (uncached NVMe): io_uring 1,417,000-1,486,000 IOPS vs linux-aio 1,322,000 IOPS (~1.07-1.12x, derived from page data) and vs synchronous read/write 814,000 IOPS (~1.74-1.83x, derived from page data). Buffered I/O (hot cache): io_uring 5,024,000 IOPS vs linux-aio 4,127,000 (~1.22x, derived from page data) and vs synchronous 4,906,000 (~1.02x, derived from page data). Optane single-CPU: io_uring 346 MB/s / 1,470us vs linux-aio 330 MB/s / 1,549us (author states ~5% faster). Author summary: 'Both io_uring and linux-aio are around twice as fast as the synchronous read interface, which in turn is twice as fast as the thread pool approach employed by posix-aio'.
hardware: 8 CPUs (exact model not stated) with NVMe storage; separate single-CPU test on Intel Optane. Kernel version and fio version not stated.
stars_or_usage: 3.8k stars; the standard userspace helper library for Linux io_uring, used by fio, QEMU, RocksDB, ScyllaDB/Seastar, and many other async-I/O consumers
tradeoffs: Linux-only (5.1+ kernel, more features on newer kernels); API is substantially more complex than read/write or epoll; io_uring has had a number of kernel-side CVEs, leading some distros/hardened environments (e.g. some container platforms, ChromeOS, and Google's production fleet historically) to disable or restrict it by default. One small vendored kernel header is GPL-with-Linux-syscall-note-exception rather than the LGPL/MIT dual license covering the rest of the repo.
caveats: The canonical evidence (Jens Axboe's 'Efficient IO with io_uring' paper at kernel.dk/io_uring.pdf) could not be opened this session due to a TLS certificate/hostname mismatch on kernel.dk, and an LWN.net article covering the same era explicitly states no benchmark numbers had been published yet at that time. Used instead a well-known independent (ScyllaDB) blog benchmark; it names the fio methodology and workload precisely but omits exact CPU model, kernel version, fio version, and compiler flags, so capped at Tier B. Gains over libaio are modest (~7-22%) and workload/queue-depth dependent; the larger win is over synchronous read/write and especially thread-pool POSIX-aio.

name: LZ4
workload: Single-thread in-memory compression/decompression speed and ratio on the Silesia corpus, using lzbench.
claimed_speedup: LZ4 default (v1.9.0): 780 MB/s compression, 4970 MB/s decompression, ratio 2.101 vs zlib deflate 1.2.11 -1: 100 MB/s compression, 415 MB/s decompression, ratio 2.730 (~7.8x faster compression, ~12.0x faster decompression, derived from page data, at a lower ratio). vs Snappy 1.1.4: 565 MB/s / 1950 MB/s, ratio 2.091 (LZ4 ~1.38x faster compression, ~2.55x faster decompression, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: GCC v8.2.0 (via lzbench's standard build; exact optimization flags not individually enumerated in the README)
stars_or_usage: 12.1k stars; used in Linux kernel, ZFS, FreeBSD, and many package/container systems
tradeoffs: Lower compression ratio than zlib/zstd in exchange for very high speed, especially decompression; LZ4_HC trades compression speed for ratio while keeping decompression speed constant; acceleration factor tunable.
caveats: License is mixed: the `lib/` directory (the actual codec) is BSD-2-Clause, while other files including the CLI are GPL-2.0-or-later — record accordingly if only the library is embedded. Benchmark tool (lzbench) is open source but numbers reported first-party in the README; compiler version, CPU, and OS are stated though exact flags are not individually listed, so treated as Tier A.

name: Zstandard (zstd)
workload: In-memory compression/decompression speed and ratio on the Silesia compression corpus, single-thread, using lzbench.
claimed_speedup: zstd 1.5.7 -1: 510 MB/s compression, 1550 MB/s decompression, ratio 2.896 vs zlib 1.3.1 -1: 105 MB/s compression, 390 MB/s decompression, ratio 2.743 (~4.9x faster compression, ~4.0x faster decompression, derived from page data, at a better ratio). vs brotli 1.1.0 -1: 290 MB/s / 425 MB/s, ratio 2.883 (zstd ~1.8x faster compression, ~3.6x faster decompression, derived from page data, comparable ratio). zstd --fast=4: 665 MB/s / 2050 MB/s vs zlib -1 (~6.3x / ~5.3x, derived from page data).

name: abseil (absl::flat_hash_map, Swiss tables)
workload: uint64_t- and std::string-keyed maps, 1-2 million entries; build+destroy, find, churn (erase+insert), and iterate ops measured via unordered_dense's third-party benchmark harness.
claimed_speedup: u64 keys: 4.25x faster build+destroy (18.50ns vs 78.66ns/op), 2.43x faster find (23.82ns vs 57.89ns/op), 3.52x faster churn (68.23ns vs 240.49ns/op), 8.28x faster iterate (2.57ns vs 21.29ns/op) (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: clang 22.1.8, -O3, transparent huge pages (madvise), process pinned to one core, Fedora 44
stars_or_usage: 18.1k stars; used in Chromium, TensorFlow, and widely at Google
tradeoffs: SwissTable open addressing gives no pointer/reference stability on rehash or erase, unlike std::unordered_map's node-based stability; resident memory is roughly on par with std (CSV 'rss' row: absl 1.11x vs std 0.94x-1.06x depending on metric).
caveats: Numbers come from a third-party harness (unordered_dense project's scripts/ab), not abseil's own repo; ratios computed by dividing the CSV's ns/op figures for the 'absl' and 'std' rows on the same page (marked derived). Standard-library implementation (libstdc++ vs libc++) is not explicitly named, only 'clang 22.1.8'. Abseil release tested was LTS 20250814, not necessarily current HEAD.

name: simdjson
workload: Full-validating JSON parsing throughput (GB/s) on real-world and synthetic JSON files (e.g. twitter.json, files from 300 bytes to 3MB), single core
claimed_speedup: "parse JSON 4x faster than RapidJSON and 25x faster than JSON for Modern C++ (nlohmann)"; also "uses three-quarters less instructions than ... RapidJSON"; NDJSON multithreaded parsing exceeds 3 GB/s
compiler_and_flags: GNU GCC 10 with -O3 (main GB/s-vs-file-type chart); GNU GCC 9 with -O3 (file-size scaling chart)
stars_or_usage: 24.3k stars; used in Node.js, ClickHouse, Meta Velox, Apache Doris, Milvus, StarRocks, WatermelonDB, Ladybird Browser
tradeoffs: The On-Demand API can drop to a fraction of its peak throughput when JSON keys arrive out of the schema's expected order or objects have variable shape (documented independently by Glaze's ABC test, which measured simdjson On-Demand at 89 MB/s vs 1163 MB/s in-order); requires padded input buffers; DOM API trades some flexibility for predictable random access.
caveats: The headline '4x RapidJSON / 25x nlohmann' figures sit at the top of the README as a general claim; the chart with fully stated methodology (GCC10/-O3, Skylake 3.4GHz) further down is captioned as comparing 'against the best and fastest C++ libraries' (which plausibly includes RapidJSON but the caption does not explicitly re-list nlohmann, which is much slower and less likely to be the 'fastest' comparison set) -- treat the two claims as related but not proven to be numerically identical to one figure. simdjson also links a dedicated reproducible-experiments repo (simdjson/simdjson_experiments_vldb2019, confirmed public but archived) for the VLDB 2019 paper underlying these results.

name: yyjson
workload: Parse and stringify twitter.json (616.7KB) at GB/s, DOM API, single-threaded, benchmarked via the separate yyjson_benchmark harness across multiple platforms/compilers/datasets
claimed_speedup: On AWS EC2 (AMD EPYC 7R32, gcc 9.3): yyjson(insitu) 1.80 GB/s parse / 1.51 GB/s stringify vs rapidjson(insitu) 0.77 GB/s parse (~2.3x), rapidjson(utf8) 0.26 GB/s parse / 0.39 GB/s stringify (~6.9x / ~3.9x), simdjson 1.52 GB/s parse / 0.61 GB/s stringify (~1.18x / ~2.5x), cjson 0.32 GB/s parse / 0.17 GB/s stringify (~5.6x / ~8.9x). On Apple A14 (clang 12), similar margins: yyjson 2.39-3.51 GB/s vs simdjson 2.19 GB/s, rapidjson 0.30-0.75 GB/s, cjson 0.48 GB/s.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 9.3 (CMake Release config) for the EC2 table; clang 12 (Release) for the Apple A14 table; interactive linked reports additionally cover msvc 2019 and clang 10 (flags are the CMake default Release optimization level, not spelled out as an explicit -O flag)
hardware: AWS EC2 c5a.large (AMD EPYC 7R32) and Apple A14 (iPhone 12 Pro) for the two tables shown in the README; additional platforms (Intel Core i5-8259U NUC, Graviton2 ARM64) covered in linked interactive charts
stars_or_usage: 3.9k stars; "The fastest JSON library in C" per repo description
tradeoffs: Arrays/objects use a linked-list-like internal structure, so indexed access is slower than sequential iterator access; parsed documents are immutable (a mutable copy is required to modify); ANSI C89 with no explicit SIMD intrinsics, trading some raw peak throughput for portability vs simdjson.
caveats: The interactive benchmark charts linked from the README are dated 'last updated 2020-12-12'; build uses CMake 'Release' config rather than an explicitly printed compiler flag string. README itself notes simdjson's newer On-Demand API can beat yyjson when most fields are known at compile time -- this benchmark only exercises the DOM APIs of both.

name: glaze
workload: Round-trip read/write of a nested JSON test struct (mixed arrays, objects, strings, numbers), 1,000,000 iterations, single core, MacBook Pro M1
claimed_speedup: Glaze 1.01s roundtrip / 1396 MB/s write / 1200 MB/s read vs RapidJSON 3.76s / 289 MB/s / 416 MB/s (~3.7x roundtrip, ~4.8x write, ~2.9x read); vs nlohmann 15.44s / 86 MB/s / 81 MB/s (~15x roundtrip); read throughput edges out simdjson On-Demand (1200 MB/s vs 1163 MB/s, ~1.03x); on Glaze's 'ABC' out-of-order-keys test, Glaze reads at 1219 MB/s vs simdjson On-Demand's 89 MB/s (~13.7x)
compiler_and_flags: Clang 17 (optimization flags not stated)
stars_or_usage: 3k stars
tradeoffs: Relies on C++20 aggregate reflection (or C++23/26 P2996 reflection on supporting compilers) rather than macros; header-only with format-specific headers to bound compile time; no exceptions/RTTI required (compiles with -fno-exceptions/-fno-rtti), which changes error-handling ergonomics vs exception-based parsers.
caveats: Benchmark is first-party: run and published by Glaze's own author in a companion repo (json_performance), using a test schema and workload the same author designed; compiler version and machine are stated but optimization flags are not, so per the tiering rules ('project's own benchmark code with partial methodology is C, not B') this caps at C even though hardware+compiler are given. The simdjson comparison specifically exercises a known weak case for simdjson's On-Demand API (out-of-order/variable keys), which the same non-neutral author highlights.

name: xsimd
workload: None found -- checked README.md, docs/source/*.rst (including vectorized_code.rst), the benchmark/ directory, and the original author's pre-xsimd blog series
claimed_speedup: No numeric claim found; only qualitative statements such as SIMD instructions "significantly accelerate code execution" and xsimd provides "accelerated implementation of common mathematical functions"
stars_or_usage: 2.8k stars; adopted by Mozilla Firefox, Apache Arrow, Pandas, KDE Krita, Meta Velox, Milvus, Pythran
tradeoffs: Requires explicit handling of the tail/remainder loop for sizes not divisible by the SIMD width; the portable API spans many ISAs (SSE/AVX/AVX512/NEON/SVE/RVV/WASM/VSX) which trades some architecture-specific peak performance for a single uniform interface.
caveats: The repo ships a benchmark/ directory (main.cpp, xsimd_benchmark.hpp) but it contains only Google-Benchmark-style harness code with no published results committed to the repo or docs. The project's documentation (readthedocs) and README are purely API/usage-focused with no performance section. The original author's 2014 blog post 'Performance Considerations About SIMD Wrappers' (predecessor project to xsimd) was checked directly and contains only assembly-level qualitative discussion, no timing numbers. Recorded at tier D per the rule for notable projects with no located numeric comparison.

name: xxHash
workload: Bandwidth (GB/s) and small-data velocity of hashing in-RAM buffers, measured with the project's open-source bench program (tests/bench).
claimed_speedup: XXH3 (AVX2) 59.4 GB/s vs City64 22.0 GB/s (~2.7x) and City128 21.7 GB/s (~2.7x), both derived from page data; also vs MurmurHash Murmur3 (32-bit) 3.9 GB/s (~15.2x, derived from page data; note Murmur3 row is the 32-bit variant, so not a perfectly matched width comparison against XXH3's 64/128-bit output). Small-data velocity: XXH3 133.1 vs City64 76.6, vs Murmur3 56.1.
compiler_and_flags: Clang v10.0, -O3
stars_or_usage: 11.3k stars
tradeoffs: XXH3/XXH128 use vectorized (SSE2/AVX2) code paths so peak numbers depend on target ISA; not a cryptographic hash (explicitly documented); 32-bit XXH32 exists for constrained targets but is far slower than XXH3.
caveats: Benchmark is first-party (project's own bench program) though methodology, compiler, flags, and CPU are fully stated, meeting Tier A. Table does not include std::hash (a listed baseline) directly, only CityHash and MurmurHash competitors; std::hash implementations vary by stdlib and are generally FNV/Murmur-derived so real-world gaps track the Murmur3 row.

name: wyhash
workload: Bulk hashing speed (MiB/sec) and cycles/hash over SMHasher's standard corpus, run on the default reference machine.
claimed_speedup: wyhash 22,640.53 MiB/s vs xxh3 20,853.74 MiB/s (~1.09x, derived from page data); vs City64 14,390.09 MiB/s (~1.57x, derived from page data); vs Murmur3A 3,027.30 MiB/s (~7.5x, derived from page data).
hardware: Default reference machine: AMD Ryzen 5 3350G 3.6GHz (per the linked sortable results table); compiler/flags not stated in the README table itself
stars_or_usage: 1.1k stars; default hash of Zig, V, Nim, and Go (since 1.17); used in abseil's low_level_hash.h and Windows Terminal
tradeoffs: No patent grant (Unlicense/public-domain dedication). Author states wyhash/wyrand are not fully 64-bit collision resistant (~62 bits) and wyrand can fail PractRand on very long (32TB) streams. wyhash's own README states the project 'has evolved into rapidhash', its successor, so new adopters are steered elsewhere.
caveats: wyhash's own README/repo contains no benchmark table; the numeric win over xxHash comes from the independent rurban/smhasher shootout, a well-known third-party suite, which states the CPU (AMD Ryzen 5 3350G) but not compiler/flags in the text reviewed, capping this at Tier B rather than A. Margin over xxh3 is narrow (~9%) and workload/CPU dependent; other CPUs in the same suite's linked tables may reorder these two.

name: Dragonbox
workload: Converting each of a 1.7M-value pool of random doubles (reduced to 1-17 significant digits) to a shortest round-trip decimal string via jkj::dragonbox::to_chars_n (full cache table) vs. std::to_chars, measured with Google Benchmark; mean time per conversion.
claimed_speedup: 1.77x faster than std::to_chars per double (28.95ns vs 51.35ns; derived from page data); also 25.723x faster than sprintf (744.72ns), directly stated in the same table
compiler_and_flags: Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.0.123.102); CMake default Release build type (CMakeLists.txt sets CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release for optimized code; exact -O flag not printed in the results table itself)
stars_or_usage: 818 stars; algorithm is used internally by {fmt} and (via fmt) by many downstream projects for double-to-string conversion
tradeoffs: Always produces the shortest round-trip representation in scientific-notation form (e.g. 0.1 -> 1E-1), not fixed-point %f-style output, so callers need extra formatting logic for printf-like output; the library's policy-based template API can cause binary bloat if many policy combinations are instantiated; header for the core algorithm is separate from the to_chars string-generation layer.
caveats: Dragonbox's own README benchmarks Grisu-Exact, Ryu and Schubfach, not std::to_chars/printf/strtod directly, so it does not by itself satisfy the WHAT COUNTS rule; this record instead relies on the independent, third-party fmtlib/dtoa-benchmark suite which does include a to_chars column. The to_chars-relative ratio is derived (both numbers are on the page, ratio computed here); single-hardware-sample (Apple M1 Pro); 'Release' build config confirmed via CMakeLists.txt rather than printed alongside the results. Last commit is just over 12 months old, hence 'stale' rather than 'active'.

name: fast_float
workload: Parsing 64-bit IEEE-754 floating point numbers with fast_float::from_chars vs. the system strtod (glibc, default locale) over three datasets - a 111k-line real-world 'canada' JSON coordinate corpus, synthetic uniform floats in [0,1), and synthetic 32-bit integers - run single-threaded on four different CPU architectures (millions of floats/sec).
claimed_speedup: 'Three to five times faster than the strtod function available in the GNU standard library... often more than twice as fast as the state-of-the-art abseil library' (verbatim from paper Section 12); e.g. Table 9, Intel Skylake, canada dataset: 45 Mfloat/s (fast_float) vs 9.0 Mfloat/s (strtod) = 5x (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: GNU GCC 10.2, full optimization (-O3 -DNDEBUG), single-threaded, run inside a privileged Ubuntu 20.10 Docker container on Linux
hardware: Intel Core i7-6700 (Skylake x64, 3.7GHz effective); also tested on AMD EPYC 7262 (Zen2 x64, 3.39GHz), an Ampere ARM server (Skylark aarch64, 3.2GHz), and IBM POWER9 (ppc64le, 3.77GHz) - see Table 8/9 of the paper
stars_or_usage: 2.1k stars; part of GCC 12's std::from_chars, and used in Chromium, WebKit/Safari, MySQL, DuckDB, Boost JSON, Blender, Apache Arrow, Google Jsonnet, ClickHouse
tradeoffs: Only supports float/double (and, with recent extensions, fixed-width float16/32/64/bfloat16) and integer types, not long double; header-only by design so adds compile-time/include overhead vs a plain libc call; locale-independent by default (needs from_chars_advanced for locale-style decimal separators).
caveats: Peer-reviewed paper (Daniel Lemire, Software: Practice and Experience 51(8), 2021); benchmark code is published separately at github.com/lemire/simple_fastfloat_benchmark (git tag v0.1.0) and github.com/fastfloat/fast_float, both opened this session. Comparison is against glibc's strtod specifically (GCC/Linux did not yet ship std::from_chars for floats at time of writing), not against libc++ or MSVC STL implementations, so Windows/macOS ratios may differ.

name: Ryu
workload: Converting each of a 1.7M-value pool of random doubles (reduced to 1-17 significant digits) to a shortest round-trip decimal string via Ryu's d2s_buffered vs. C sprintf("%.17g", value), measured with Google Benchmark; mean time per conversion.
claimed_speedup: 16.164x faster than sprintf per double (46.07ns vs 744.72ns), directly stated in the benchmark table
compiler_and_flags: Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.0.123.102); CMake default Release build type (CMakeLists.txt sets CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release for optimized code; exact -O flag not printed in the results table itself)
stars_or_usage: 1.4k stars; ported to Rust (dtolnay/ryu), Go, Julia (in the Julia standard library), Zig, C#, D, Scala, Erlang/OTP, Haskell bytestring; algorithm published in peer-reviewed PLDI'18 and OOPSLA'19 papers
tradeoffs: C implementation (plus a Java port); the highly optimized paths only cover 32/64-bit float/double, with a slower generic 128-bit fallback for long double/__float128; Ryu Printf only implements %f/%e precision formatting, not the full printf flag set.
caveats: Ryu's own README claims larger wins (15x-24x) for Ryu Printf vs. various platform libc printf implementations (glibc, musl, MSVC, Apple libc), but states no CPU model, only OS/libc versions, so that first-party claim is Tier C on its own. This record instead cites the independent, reproducible fmtlib/dtoa-benchmark comparison (compiler+hardware stated) against C sprintf, which shows a smaller but still large (16.164x) win. Single-hardware-sample (Apple M1 Pro); 'Release' build config confirmed via CMakeLists.txt rather than printed alongside the results.

name: {fmt}
workload: Converting each of a 1.7M-value pool of random doubles (reduced to 1-17 significant digits) to a shortest round-trip decimal string via fmt::format_to with compile-time format strings, measured with Google Benchmark; mean time per conversion.
claimed_speedup: 20.214x faster than sprintf per double (36.84ns vs 744.72ns); ~24x faster than ostringstream (885.30ns) (derived from page data); fmt README separately states '{fmt} can be tens of percent to 20-30x faster than sprintf and iostreams, especially for numeric formatting'
compiler_and_flags: Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.0.123.102); CMake default Release build type (CMakeLists.txt sets CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release for optimized code; exact -O flag not printed in the results table itself)
stars_or_usage: 25.8k stars; used in FoundationDB, Ceph, ClickHouse, Envoy, Battle.net, and the reference implementation basis for C++20 std::format
tradeoffs: Adds a header-only or compiled dependency vs. printf; compiles noticeably slower than raw printf (5.1s vs 1.6s for the bloat-test suite) though far faster than IOStreams (25.5s); template-heavy formatting machinery can grow binary size if many format-string/type combinations are instantiated; requires C++11+.
caveats: The exact numbers come from the fmtlib/dtoa-benchmark repo (linked from the fmt README's Performance section) rather than being pasted directly into the fmt README; the fmt README's own separate compile-time table (Apple M5 Max, Apple Clang 21.0.0, -O3) shows a different comparison (compile time/binary size, not speed) so was not used here. Single-hardware-sample (Apple M1 Pro) result; 'Release' build config was confirmed by reading CMakeLists.txt rather than being printed alongside the results table.

name: xoshiro/xoroshiro generators
workload: Shootout table (harness.c timing + PAPI cycle counts) measuring nanoseconds to emit 64 random bits and cycles/byte for each generator on a single core, including MT19937-64 and xoshiro256++/xoroshiro128++.
claimed_speedup: xoshiro256++: 0.75 ns/64 bits, 0.34 cycles/byte vs MT19937-64: 1.36 ns/64 bits, 0.62 cycles/byte -- about 1.8x faster (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 12.2.1, -fno-unroll-loops (deliberately without -march=native, to exclude vectorization advantages)
stars_or_usage: Algorithms adopted as default PRNGs in multiple languages/runtimes (e.g. Java's java.util.random package, Rust rand_xoshiro, NumPy Generator, Lua, V8)
tradeoffs: Not cryptographically secure; xoshiro/xoroshiro fail a small number of specialized statistical tests (e.g. linear-complexity/binary-rank style tests) despite passing BigCrush overall; much shorter period than MT19937 (e.g. 2^256-1 vs 2^19937-1), which is a theoretical rather than practical concern for almost all uses.
caveats: This is an author-run first-party site (Sebastiano Vigna, co-author of the algorithms), not an independent benchmark; however the harness (harness.c, PAPI-based cycle counting) and every generator's source file are public, and CPU model, compiler, and flags are explicitly stated, meeting tier A's disclosure bar. The MT19937-64 compared against is the classical reference implementation, not confirmed to be literally std::mt19937_64 from libstdc++/libc++/MSVC STL, though those wrap the same core Mersenne Twister algorithm and are expected to perform similarly; no repo/commit history exists since this is a hand-maintained webpage, not a git project.

name: RE2
workload: Same NSDI'19 Hyperscan-paper experiment: total wall-clock time for single-regex serial matching (RE2-s) of Snort Talos (1,300 regexes) and Suricata ET-Open (2,800 regexes) rulesets against a 1GB real HTTP traffic trace, single CPU core.
claimed_speedup: RE2-s beats classic (non-JIT) PCRE v8.41: Talos 6942s -> 1777s (~3.9x); ET-Open 12800s -> 4696s (~2.7x) (derived from page data, Table 5). Paper explicitly states Hyperscan-s beats RE2-s by 10.3x/9.1x, implying RE2-s itself is faster than plain PCRE but far slower than PCRE2 (JIT): RE2-s (1777s/4696s) was actually slower than PCRE2 (394s/913s) in the same table, and RE2-m (1116s) was slower than PCRE2 (913s) on the larger ET-Open ruleset.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 5.4; RE2 v2018-09-01; PCRE v8.41 (non-JIT, matched one-at-a-time per RE2/PCRE's API); full optimization flags not stated.
hardware: Intel Xeon Platinum 8180 CPU @ 2.50GHz, 48GB memory, single core
stars_or_usage: 9.8k stars; used in production at Google since 2006 and widely elsewhere
tradeoffs: Linear-time guarantee (no catastrophic backtracking) trades away backreferences and lookaround; RE2's own README explicitly disclaims being a universal speed leader ('It is not a goal to be faster than all other engines under all circumstances'); in this benchmark RE2 loses outright to PCRE2's JIT compiler despite beating classic PCRE.
caveats: RE2's own repo/README and its historic benchlog files (benchlog/benchlog.c2, .mini, .r70, .wreck) only benchmark against classic PCRE on decade-old hardware (e.g. AMD Opteron 8214, MacPro1,1 circa 2008-2010) with no PCRE2 or std::regex comparison at all -- PCRE2 postdates most of those logs. No first-party or independent source found this session showing RE2 beating std::regex or PCRE2 specifically; the only numeric, methodologically-documented comparison located is the third-party NSDI'19 Hyperscan paper (same source used for the Hyperscan record above), where RE2 beats classic PCRE but not PCRE2. Baseline recorded here is PCRE (not in this project's suggested baseline list of std::regex/PCRE2), so baseline_in_list=false per the hard rules.
found_via: seed-record pass: data/wave0-seed/prompts/seed-05-regex-conc.txt; NSDI'19 paper https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi19/presentation/wang-xiang; RE2 repo benchlog/ and README checked directly for a std::regex/PCRE2 comparison but found none

name: CTRE (compile-time regular expressions)
workload: Raw `time`-command wall-clock comparison of egrep, CTRE, PCRE, and std::regex matching four regex patterns (e.g. 'ABCD|DEFGH|EFGHI|A{4,}', '[0-9a-fA-F]{8,16}', '^([0-9]{4,16})?[aA]', '([aAbB]{4,}|[xXyY]{4,}|[1234]{4,})0'), captured once with clang (clang-bench.txt) and once with gcc (gcc-bench.txt). No description of input size, test harness, or what program was actually timed.
claimed_speedup: clang-bench.txt: CTRE 10.093s vs std::regex 21m9.309s (~125x) on 'ABCD|DEFGH|EFGHI|A{4,}'; CTRE 14.197s vs std::regex 2m34.505s (~10.9x) on '[0-9a-fA-F]{8,16}'; CTRE 7.596s vs std::regex 7m54.793s (~62.5x) on '^([0-9]{4,16})?[aA]'; CTRE 59.864s vs std::regex 27m35.004s (~27.6x) on the alternation pattern. gcc-bench.txt shows smaller but still large gaps, e.g. CTRE 3.982s vs std::regex 0m55.058s (~13.8x) on the first pattern.
compiler_and_flags: clang (version unstated) for clang-bench.txt, gcc (version unstated) for gcc-bench.txt; no optimization flags stated.
stars_or_usage: 3.9k stars; used as a reference implementation for a C++ standards proposal (P1433) for compile-time regex
tradeoffs: Regex pattern must be a compile-time-known string (template/NTTP); needs recent compilers (clang 14+, gcc 9+, MSVC 16.11+); does not support callouts, comments, conditional patterns, control-char escapes, named characters, octal numbers, subroutines, or Unicode grapheme-cluster \X (per README's PCRE-syntax exception list).
caveats: Current README (v3) contains zero benchmark numbers, and the compile-time.re site's dedicated 'Performance graph' page (/graph/) is JS-rendered client-side and its underlying data could not be extracted via WebFetch this session. The only numeric evidence found is two stale, undocumented repo files (clang-bench.txt / gcc-bench.txt) with no compiler version, flags, hardware, or input description, and several ratios exceed 50x -- per the hard rules this unstated-methodology + implausible-ratio combination caps the tier at C. It is unclear which CTRE version/commit produced these files or whether they reflect the current v3 codebase.
found_via: seed-record pass: data/wave0-seed/prompts/seed-05-regex-conc.txt; repo files clang-bench.txt and gcc-bench.txt in github.com/hanickadot/compile-time-regular-expressions; compile-time.re homepage and /graph/ page checked for benchmarks

name: Hyperscan
workload: Total wall-clock time to match Snort Talos (1,300 regexes) and Suricata ET-Open (2,800 regexes) rulesets against a 1GB real HTTP traffic trace (818,682 packets), single CPU core, comparing PCRE, PCRE2, RE2, and Hyperscan in single-regex (-s) and multi-regex parallel (-m) modes.
claimed_speedup: Table 5 (seconds, lower=better): Talos ruleset - PCRE 6942, PCRE2 394, RE2-s 1777, Hyperscan-s 173, RE2-m 29, Hyperscan-m 2.15. ET-Open - PCRE 12800, PCRE2 913, RE2-s 4696, Hyperscan-s 516, RE2-m 1116, Hyperscan-m 133. Paper states: 'Hyperscan-s outperforms PCRE, RE2-s, and PCRE2 by 40.1x, 10.3x, and 2.3x' (Talos); 'Hyperscan-m is 13.5x faster than RE2-m while it reveals 183.3x performance improvement over PCRE2' (Talos); 'Hyperscan-s shows 24.8x, 9.1x, and 1.8x speedups over PCRE, RE2-s, and PCRE2' (ET-Open); 'Hyperscan-m outperforms RE2-m and PCRE2 by 8.4x and 6.9x' (ET-Open). Separately, Hyperscan-ported Snort achieves 986 Mbps vs 113 Mbps for stock Snort (8.73x) on the same real traffic.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 5.4; PCRE v8.41 and PCRE2 v10.32 built with JIT enabled; RE2 v2018-09-01; Hyperscan v5.0. Full optimization flags not stated.
hardware: Intel Xeon Platinum 8180 CPU @ 2.50GHz, 48GB memory, single core used for evaluation
stars_or_usage: 5.5k stars; used in Snort/Suricata-class DPI, widely deployed in network security products
tradeoffs: x86-specific (SIMD/SSE/AVX) C API; requires precompiled pattern databases (compile step separate from scan); biggest wins are in multi-pattern/large-ruleset DPI workloads (6.9-183x over PCRE2) rather than single-pattern matching (2.3x over PCRE2); streaming mode has extra overhead vs block mode.
caveats: Benchmark was run and published by the paper's authors, several of whom (Intel, branchfree.org's Geoff Langdale) are Hyperscan's own developers, so despite NSDI peer review it is not fully independent. The real-world HTTP traffic trace ('obtained at a cloud service provider') is not public, so exact reproduction needs a substitute trace; no explicit public artifact/script repo for the Snort/ruleset harness was found, only library versions and hardware/compiler, so tier capped at B rather than A. Some ratios exceed 50x (e.g. 183.3x) but compiler/hardware/library versions are stated and it is not a debug/-O0 build, so the hard-rule auto-cap-to-C does not apply.

name: Highway (vqsort)
workload: bench_sort benchmark sorting arrays of built-in types (e.g. f32, uniform32 distribution) up to 1e6 keys with AVX-512 (AVX3), comparing LLVM libc++ std::sort against vqsort, reporting output throughput in MB/s of sorted key bytes.
claimed_speedup: About 10x faster than LLVM's std::sort for large arrays of built-in types (as of 2022-06-07). README example: AVX3, f32, uniform32, 1.00E+06 keys: std::sort 54 MB/s vs vqsort 1143 MB/s (~21x on that specific case, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Clang (tested with 13.0.1 and 15.0.6), Bazel `-c opt` optimized build
stars_or_usage: 5.9k stars; used in Google projects and backed by a peer-reviewed paper (arXiv:2205.05982)
tradeoffs: Full speedup needs SIMD-capable hardware (AVX2/AVX3/NEON/SVE) with runtime dispatch; not a stable sort; speedup magnitude varies a lot by instruction set, key type, and distribution; small-array performance was a later optimization added after the original headline number.
caveats: The README itself notes pdqsort-class scalar algorithms are 'about twice as fast as LLVM's std::sort' (as of 2023-06), so the 10x figure is specifically vs plain std::sort, not vs the best scalar competitor. Independent analysis by Lukas Bergdoll (sort-research-rs) found a performance bug (entropy fetched from the OS on every call) that was fixed in PR #1334 after the original numbers were published; some published figures predate that fix.

name: pdqsort
workload: Median cycle counts (bench.cpp) sorting arrays of built-in types under multiple input distributions (random, ascending, descending, all-equal, etc.), compared to GCC's std::sort and std::stable_sort.
claimed_speedup: Faster than GCC's std::sort/std::stable_sort across tested distributions; exact ratios are shown only in a bar-chart image linked from the README, not as text/table values on the page.
compiler_and_flags: g++ -std=c++11 -O2 -m64 -march=native (per README)
stars_or_usage: 2.5k stars; algorithm concepts adopted in Rust's sort_unstable and referenced widely in later stdlib sort redesigns
tradeoffs: Not stable (no stable variant provided); branchless fast path only applies to arithmetic types with default std::less/std::greater; falls back to heapsort on adversarial inputs.
caveats: Benchmark numbers only appear as a bar-chart image (i.imgur.com/1RnIGBO.png); no numeric claimed_speedup could be read as text, so this could not be verified against the hard rule requiring numbers to appear on the page as text. A CPU label ('i5-4670k @ 3.4GHz') appears only as an example argument to the post-processing script in bench/readme.txt, not a firm statement that this was the machine used for the published graph, so hardware is recorded as unstated. Repo has had no commits since 2021-03-14 (>3 years), capping maintenance_status at abandoned despite the algorithm remaining influential.

name: ska_sort
workload: Nanoseconds-per-item sorting of integers, floats, structs (128-1024 bytes), and strings via radix sort / American flag sort (ska_sort), compared against std::sort across increasing array sizes and skewed distributions.
claimed_speedup: Author's blog post claims ska_sort is 'twice as fast as std::sort for many inputs' once arrays exceed roughly 128 elements, with much larger gains on skewed/geometric-distributed integer data ('many times faster').
stars_or_usage: 248 stars
tradeoffs: Not a comparison sort; requires an extractable radix key (integers, bit-tricked floats, strings, tuples); not stable; needs O(n) auxiliary buffer memory; benefit shrinks for very large keys or non-radix-friendly types.
caveats: The GitHub repo itself ships only ska_sort.hpp and a test/benchmark .cpp file with no README and no numbers; the only detailed claimed_speedup lives in the author's 2016 blog post, which states no compiler, flags, or CPU model, so this is a first-party claim with partial methodology (tier C). Repo has had no commits since 2017-05-15.

name: vergesort
workload: Sorting one million ints under various input distributions (shuffled, sawtooth, pipe organ, push front/middle, etc.) with random-access iterators, comparing std::sort, std::stable_sort, heapsort, pdqsort, and vergesort.
claimed_speedup: Benchmark chart shows vergesort winning on 'sawtooth' distributions with long sorted/reverse-sorted runs versus std::sort/std::stable_sort/heapsort/pdqsort; exact ratios are shown only in bar-chart images (imgur PNGs), not as text numbers on the page.
compiler_and_flags: MinGW g++ 6.1.0 -std=c++1z -O2 -march=native
stars_or_usage: 73 stars
tradeoffs: Not stable; best case relies on data containing sorted runs of size > n/log n; the bidirectional-iterator variant's worst case is O(n^2) since it falls back to a median-of-9 quicksort instead of pdqsort.
caveats: Numbers are shown only as chart images with no CPU/hardware model stated anywhere in the README or fallbacks.md, so tier is capped at C despite compiler and flags being given. Benchmarks were compiled with an older GCC (6.1.0 via MinGW), predating later pdqsort/std::sort improvements in newer compilers.
